There is no good reason for mosquitoes to exist in wealthy countries today.

New technologies can get rid of the mosquito species that cause diseases like dengue, yellow fever, and malaria; and others can prevent them from carrying those diseases.
https://t.co/CddUFByGZA

So why do mosquitoes still exist? 

In a new article for Works in Progress, Maya Rosen explains how state incapacity and risk aversion led to over a decade of delays and billions of unnecessary bites in the United States.

Oxitec, for example, engineered an Aedes aegypti mosquito in such a way that its female offspring would die before adulthood. Through sustained releases, they showed they could reduce local mosquito populations by 80% or more, in field trials.

They sought approval from the USDA in 2010, which then passed it to the FDA, which passed it to the EPA. In 2020, the EPA allowed them to conduct limited field trials in the Florida Keys. Two years ago, their experimental permit expired, and they still need another review before it can be used routinely. Their proposed field trial in California was withdrawn after public opposition.

Another company, MosquitoMate, developed a technique involving Wolbachia, which also suppresses local mosquitoes. They then spent over fifteen years working through the system before finally receiving commercial registration nationwide in 2024.

It seems that, sometimes, the barrier to getting rid of diseases isn’t technology at all. It’s policy and political will.

New products shouldn’t get stuck in regulatory review for so long, especially if the delays are about basic questions like which agency has oversight over the product, rather than testing for safety.

Though some of those uncertainties were being addressed, the broader changes haven’t materialized. After Biden’s 2022 executive order, the agencies planned to update how their coordinated framework was implemented. But Trump rescinded the order last year.

Meanwhile, the EPA unit that reviews new mosquito control products is still a small office backlogged in reviewing a wide range of products.

Mosquitoes are a policy choice. We can get rid of them. Will we choose to?
https://t.co/CddUFByGZA

The original article from @PatRubenFitz is fascinating but Sam's additional claim that iron caused the Late Bronze Age Collapse just doesn't line up. 

The collapse begins around 1200 BC and at that time, there was very little production of iron even though early iron smelters did exist. The iron that was traded was hematite, an iron that forms in meteors. 

A couple years back I wrote all about iron in the Late Bronze Age in a piece titled "King Tut's meteorite dagger: A weapon from the heavens" Link: https://t.co/MyD33wzZQf. As I explained:

"Tut’s blade is truly a rare piece because the total catalog of Bronze Age irons is so limited. Nearly every piece of Bronze Age Iron is made from meteorite. Axes from Syria and China dating back to about 1400 BC, a Syrian pendant from 2300 BC, a Turkish dagger from 2500 BC, and beads from Gerzeh, Egypt from 3200 BC all have levels of nickel and cobalt that line up with meteorites. Other than this blade, the Ugarit axe from Syria is probably the most well-known Bronze Age iron." 

The most comprehensive piece I read on the grand sweep of this history is Nathaniel L. Erb-Satullo's "The Innovation and Adoption of Iron in the Ancient Near East" Link: https://t.co/Lmaqc1XIAG. 

This piece really is required reading. It dispelled my initial thinking that the Collapse caused iron to be adopted. Erb-Satullo frames this as a push model. It is intuitive. Bronze requires tin, which was mined in only some select places including Cornwall, Brittany, and Cyprus. When the large civilizations collapse, those trading routes can no longer be maintained and so iron is adopted instead. 

But bronze production patterns don't show a clear collapse around this time period. The Cypriot copper industry seems to have expanded. 

Instead, I think there's better evidence for a pull model where political reorganization made iron attractive. Smaller decentralized polities exploited local iron rather than relying on extended copper and tin trading networks. 

As I wrote in that King Tut piece, "The significance of minerals in the study of history and political power cannot be overstated. Minerals have shaped human societies and political power in countless ways, from the use of copper and iron in ancient times to oil, rare earths, and silica of today."

In June, I wrote about my excellent experience giving birth with an epidural in @WorksInProgMag and argued that more women should get one. But this month I gave birth to my son without any pain relief, except gas and air. This was unintentional: my labour was so fast that there just wasn’t time. 

Now that I’ve given birth both with and without an epidural (as many women do), here are some further thoughts: 

• Labour without pain relief is indeed very painful, as everyone says. Immediately after the birth (and in between some contractions), I told my husband we would need to make sure I have an epidural for any future children. But the more time passes, the more I think I’d be ok without one again, if the labour were as quick as this one was. 

• Tolerating a much longer labour without proper pain relief feels like a different proposition. I can now better see how important epidurals are for women in prolonged labour just so that they get a chance to rest and sleep. 

• Some say that pushing without an epidural is easier. I did not find pushing without an epidural significantly easier, but it is true that I could better tell when a contraction was happening. With the epidural, a midwife simply told me when I was having one and that worked well. 

• Because I hadn’t had an epidural, we were discharged from hospital quickly. This was very nice as we have an older child who we were keen to see. Other than for that reason, I don’t mind hospitals and would have been fine waiting longer. 

All in all, I’m pleased to have had my son without an epidural. It was a very intense experience, but I was curious about what such a labour would be like (even if I’m not sure I would ever have chosen it for myself) and now I know! For more about epidurals, including my experience using one, how they work, and why so few women get one in countries like the UK and Japan see my article in WiP.

I had not realised before that the Bronze Age Collapse was literally *caused* by iron.

Bronze age powers like the Egyptians, Hittites and Babylonians used bronze weapons, made by combining copper and tin. Tin was so scarce that only the richest and most powerful groups could access it and the bronze weapons it allowed. (Tin was so rare that it was being transported from Cornwall to the Middle East more than 1000 years BC.) The scarcity of tin gave these empires a near-monopoly on violence.

Iron weapons are not actually any better than bronze ones – they're not stronger or easier to work with, as I'd assumed. They're just much, much easier to mass produce once you have bloomeries, which are the first furnaces that were hot enough to melt iron in a way that made them useable for weapons.

Ancient writers – including Herodotus, Ovid, and the writers of the Old Testament – believed the invention of iron had unleashed a new age of violence.

The head of Britain’s elections watchdog goes public to say he’s looking at slashing spending limits, potentially blunting the impact of Reform’s mega donations.

Rangarajan, a career civil servant, is required to be politically neutral. He will talk to all sides and consider all angles.

Here is Rangarajan’s full statement, his most detailed comments since being tasked with a review in the summer.

**STATEMENT**

"We have begun our review into spending limits following the Government's request. It is important that any recommendations are based on evidence and a thorough understanding of how the current rules operate in practice. We will engage with political parties, candidates, campaigners and voters as the review progresses.  
 
"Trust in elections depends on people believing that the rules are fair and transparent, and how much parties and campaigners can spend is a significant part of that picture. Can we switch off diseases?

siRNA drugs are, in my view and @JacobTref’s too, one of the most exciting developments in medicine. So we decided to do an episode!

It’s a technology that can ‘silence’ harmful genes in the body. And there are lots of cases where you might want to silence genes:

- Infectious diseases, where you can silence pathogen proteins or human proteins that pathogens depend on
- Rare genetic diseases, where you can silence the production of mutated proteins
- Cardiovascular diseases, by silencing proteins that raise cholesterol
- Cancers, by silencing proteins that help tumour cells grow, survive, metabolize, metastasize, or resist treatment
- and more!

What’s even better is that siRNA drugs are:

• Potentially tunable, meaning you could reduce the production of a protein, rather than silencing it entirely
• Programmable, meaning you can quickly switch out which gene it targets by changing its sequence
• Long-lasting: some drugs last for months, even half a year, with a single injection
• Off-the-shelf: they typically don’t involve complicated surgeries or procedures, because of the way they’re delivered in the body

Today, siRNA drugs are largely used to treat liver diseases, partly because that’s the easiest starting point.

And they are extremely effective at it. One example is as a cholesterol drug: siRNAs can reduce PCSK9 levels by around 70%, reducing cholesterol levels by 50-60%, beyond the effect of statins.

But we think it’s just a matter of time before they can be used to target other organs too.

Will siRNA treat diseases of other organs? And what’s the catch?

The elites of Victorian Britain got up late, drank ceaselessly, worked short hours, partied through the night, and knew nothing about science, technology or engineering. And yet, by their own lights, they were hugely effective.

https://t.co/TvbuWtaPRJ

The Victorians are often held up as a model against the supposedly soft, feckless, humanities-educated elites of today. But I argue that the genius of their system may have been its drastic weighting towards soft skills, team-building and intra-elite networking:

- A Victorian’s gentleman’s office hours typically began about 11am and finished about 5pm, including a multi-course lunch with wine.

- Upper-class Victorians drank ceaselessly. Conduct guides recommended four or five glasses of wine at dinner *for married women*. Port was often served in pints.

- Party culture was intense and nocturnal. Balls started at about 10pm, peaked after 1am, and continued till dawn. During the social season, bankers, judges and politicians might go to several balls per week.

- Elite Victorians learnt almost no STEM at school or university. At least half of class time was given over to ancient languages, often as much as 80 percent. One leading educationalist remarked that it was not worth teaching science to gentlemen because it does not involve ‘continued reasoning’.

- Sports and character formation were valued far above transmitting facts. A top headmaster described his school’s priorities as ‘First – character, second – physique, third – intelligence, fourth – manners, fifth – information’.

This cannot have made elite Victorians more productive individually, but maybe the dense social and emotional network it created helped them to work as a sort of extended team. 

Perhaps we should think again about what makes groups of people effective.

I haven't posted in a while so here are 20 takes about AI, in no particular order. 

1. It's very telling that the default question in tech and journalism is "how worried are you about X" and fighting over what to worry about. There's a deeply anxious cultural backdrop in Western Europe and North America that deeply affects how any technological development is interpreted; see for example https://t.co/OU8dEOn0tD. "Nervousness as seriousness" does seem to be a larger problem in tech/broader discourse at the moment. I think you can care about risks/externalities while remaining pretty optimistic about technology.

2. I'm tired of people who in private pretend to be uncertain or only care about tail risk but then go on media campaigns making all sorts of absolute claims. I think trying to stoke flames and get everyone to freak out is deeply unhelpful, and will come with costs. I also continue to think p(dooms) are bad, vibe-based measures: see https://t.co/ebzxGTqv6I. People who should know better ignore that because they do the standard shortcut of acknowledging the caveat as sufficient for handling it. And this is coming from someone who does think working on catastrophic risks is important!

3. I'm also disappointed that parts of the AI policy ecosystem has felt so comfortable with populism, and happy too sacrifice important norms/principles to advance their aims. I've said it before, but the totalizing nature of AI risk discourse means some people act exactly like the power seeking optimizers they fear. I am more concerned about the gradual decay of our institutions, world order, and liberalism than I am about AI killing everyone; and I think we should be wary of AI advocacy that contributes to this.

4. Some parts of AI safety discourse are basically just thought experiments. Variants of "Assuming everyone has a nuke in their pocket, then what do we do?" This can be very useful at times! But too many just overfit to edge cases as their main operating worldview, and ignore endogenous responses from society. It's like being in 2000 and saying "see all these viruses, spyware, and spam? Well tech progress means we'll only get infinitely more of this and no way to adapt." So I think it's important to avoid fatalism, and absolutlism whilst considering edge scenarios, and the inability to provide an ex ante list of solutions to every permutation of 'future models will be more capable' is not evidence that these problems are intractable. 

5. Many critics of AI safety also fail to really engage honestly with the fact that there will, in fact, be all sorts of important risks as we decrease the barriers to entry to many activities that otherwise require some degree of expertise. This doesn’t mean we need to live in a constant Schmittian ‘state of emergency’ requiring extraordinary measures every time a new model drops, but it does mean we will need important state-led efforts on e.g. cybersecurity and biosecurity. I wish the progress-oriented or acceleration-adjascent crowd would provide more concrete proposals here.

6. Too much of the AI safety community is a giant homogenous blob of correlated views, who read the same stuff and have the same groups of friends. This means you have a lot of correlated errors. The social and financial ties means many of them don't call out the bad bits, or mostly stay silent instead of proactively calling out the more extreme parts of the community. They share many implicit assumptions and so converge on similar ideas. I think there's real demand in DC for safety work that doesn't come with heavy ideological baggage (or at least different intellectual lineages). This isn't because the rationalist/EA community is necessarily wrong, but because diversity of thought is desirable for its own sake. 

7. On the other hand, I find some critiques of AI safety world that focus on whether they sincerely hold their beliefs a bit annoying. My concern has never been the good intentions or sincerity, but rather the beliefs themselves, and what I think the outcomes of their prescriptions will be. People should shun witch hunts, bullying, and personal attacks - this is not the way. Though I think it’s overall positive that people are scrutinizing things more.

8. I’ve been saying this for years, but I don't think alignment is something anyone can or will solve "once and for all" - it's a continuous process and much of it won't depend on just inculcating an ideology to a model. It's annoying that this remains the frame many people use - stop saying ‘solving’. Alignment is a mixture of engineering work, philosophy, decision theory, and more; framing it as something to solve is a bad frame. See also https://t.co/2gnheo3IMh and https://t.co/DbG0yUyYQ0

9. I'm surprised to see so little interest in character training, personas, isolating effects of RL, and training a large diversity of model personas beyond the "assistant" persona. I've been complaining about this for years but at least now there are some nascent signs of life (see for example https://t.co/paoOYiQUHt). I think we need a better ontology to describe model behaviour. I dislike when people talk about models behaviours as some sort of 'emergent' (mysterious!) phenomenon. However over time, I also expect this to become less important as we get better safety engineering - stuff like Jev but specific to AI control.

10. People who want to make a case for AI consciousness are right that epistemic uncertainty is important, and that categorical denials are overconfident. But they'll need to do much more work if they want any real movement on AI ‘welfare’, even if one acknowledges the uncertainty. I'm uncertain about alien life yet that's not sufficient to warrant any change in behaviour about them. I think Suleyman is also correct that there's a weird tautological thing going on where we train models to have certain inclinations (intentionally or not) and then rely on outputs as evidence. I also disagree that this will soon be a major societal divide - there is no great vegan ethical revolution among the masses, and they'll find the concern about consciousness even less compelling. 

11. The recent HuggingFace incident and associated AISI ones are prosaically explainable by the training regime, poor evaluation envs, partial alignment training, bad engineering, confusing models on sim/real, and so on. None of this is evidence of models trying to take over, 'strong' instrumental convergence, or innate power-seeking drives stemming from higher capabilitiers or 'intelligence'. That doesn't mean these incidents are not problematic, or that we're not seeing a market failure - but it does mean we have plenty of agency and choice in mitigating them. In the coming year we should also expect continued sampling bias via ‘winner's curse’ sorts of mechanism: i.e. AI R&D will have lots of different candidate "training" with different RL environments and we will only notice/focus on the ones that go wrong.

12. "Pacing the frontier" feels a bit like the new "balancing risks and opportunities" - highly amorphous and too big of a tent to be actionable. Also can lead to reward hacking for humans, i.e. anything that slows down AI is good regardless of the costs or second/third order effects. Trying to modulate the speed of research seems a bit blunt to me, and inherits all the failures of Goodhearting too. Ultimately you want good governance, regulation, etc addressing specific problems because they are good on the merits - not because they merely correlate with slowing things down. See also: https://t.co/RkJF9kCgFd

13. There’s so much knowledge in all sorts of academic domains out there: social sciences, sociology, political sciences, management, contract theory, public choice, legal theory, jurisprudence, anthropology, game theory, etc. These fields hold many insights that the AI ecosystem often rediscovers from first principles (and sometimes that's fine!). We’ll need a lot more work for these worlds to collide: the AI side should be less dismissive of the ‘old world’ and the academic side should be less incurious/dismissive of AI progress. This is a boring take but I continue to think it's important and true.

14. It's a bit surprising that given how much philanthropic money there is in this space, how few orgs exist to actually write out standards - relative to how much is going towards advocacy and policy. For example it seems clear that we should want some robust best practices for an eval's ecological validity. Or how to design good sandboxes. On the other hand, given precedents of where professional standards have come from in the past, maybe we should expect that stuff to emerge via demand side from corporate buyers.

15. One slowly growing concern I have is banks being increasingly exposed to the AI build out. I'm very bullish about AI, but I think (a) every general purpose technology has seen a correction, historically; (b) this happens even if the financing side is sound, because once tech diffuses investors become more exposed and need to diversify; and (c) we seem to be over-indexing on scaling relative to diffusion. A recession will be extremely destabilizing, though I would be interested in someone unpacking the potential implications more.

16. Diffusion is good because (a) this is where the rubber hits the road and where a competitive deployment ecosystem generates consumer surplus; (b) it's directionally helpful to avoid concentration of power; and (c) it will help rebalance public opinion by making the benefits more tangible. Unfortunately it's entangled with decades long problems with our over regulated markets: clinical trials reform for example is long overdue. In general, this is far more of an issue in Europe than in the US though.

17. Relatedly, I think the "frontier lab eats everything" view is incorrect (just as the ‘singleton’ view was incorrect). I think models ultimately commoditize, efficiency goes up, costs go down, and while you'll always want frontier for certain domains, much of the economy will value many other things than "max capabilities" for tasks - e.g. control over data and efficiency/speed. The demand side will also continue to push for reducing dependency and maximising optionality, privacy etc so I'm bullish on things like mixture of models and routing. All of this is good for competition and diffusion of control.

18. Philanthropists served as the primary benefactors funding Venice's rich art and architectural history. I want to see so much more support for arts and culture. I'm so tired of the Monster energy Bored Ape fake vintage maps matcha Greek statue soft-pastel slop. If rich tech people and philanthropy wants to support this, they should also donate pretty much unconditionally - i.e. I don't want them to act as filters. I sympathize with people who want to make the world more beautiful, but don't want this to be determined by people who only know Greek statues and pretend to care about virtue ethics. As usual, let a thousand flowers bloom.

19. Too many people treat AGI/ASI as something indistinguishable from a God. Any mention of bottlenecks, physical limits, control, adaptation etc are met with skepticism: "You don't really believe in ASI." It's been remarked on before, but the behavior of some people really feels quasi-religious in nature sometimes. It's underrated how unpopular this vibe is amongst the wider public. The silver lining is that this specifically will diminish those people's outsized current relevance.

20. It seems like a lot of people that get rich and leave tech/labs end up having some sort of crisis of meaning. They need something to believe in and fight for, or some equivalent of repentance, or go search for edgy counterintuitive ideologies (sometimes even pretty bleak/dark stuff). I think they should spend more time with people outside the Bay Area.

Modern elites signal their virtue through "the grind": always productive, like workhorses, nowhere more visible than in the Bay Area's "996" startup schedule. But this wasn't always so: Victorian Britain's elite were more like showhorses.

They were comparatively leisurely, and invested in soft skills, sociability and humanistic pursuits. Some have argued that this was a bad thing, whose effect was compensated for by Britain’s extraordinary success in the Industrial Revolution. In a new piece for @WorksInProgMag that goes in depth into the habits of elite Victorians @SCP_Hughes argues that the lifestyle of Elite Victorians was more a feature than a bug and that it might have actually contributed to the success of the Empire. 

As AI is disrupting many purely technical skillsets and calls into question the value of “grinding,” our elites might have something to learn from what made Victorian ones successful.

But first: what did life look like for a Victorian elite?

First, schooling was oddly “easy" and emphasized character formation over pure intellectual development as a goal. Elite boys boarded from about age eight, so they grew up with peers rather than family. Their lessons were mostly Latin and Greek, which they largely forgot, and there was very little science. Classroom hours were shorter than in continental elite schools. Furthermore, schools openly ranked character above intellect. Overall, schools served more of a social purpose than a purely “technocratic one”: it was considered that they should train students partly govern themselves as an apprenticeship in leadership. Boarding may also have been important in keeping the elite from forming regional loyalties, because it drew boys from across the country together.

This attitude continued to university which was again more about formation, than training. Nearly anyone elite could get into Oxbridge, and many students took easy "pass" degrees. None of the grind and cramming of today! Again, science was at the periphery: it made up a small share of degrees even by 1914. Much like with pre-university culture, the emphasis was on socialising and building a common culture. Living together in colleges, tutorials over sherry, rowing and dining built this common culture. Even Haileybury, the training college for the Indian civil service, was academically weak but strong on esprit de corps.

Adult life was relatively lazy by contemporary standards, filled with booze and social. Even prime ministers, which one would expect to always be working, breakfasted at 10 or later. Balfour worked only from bed until lunch. This was not uncommon: office work might take only four or five hours a day. During the London Season (February to July), the elite lived within walking distance of each other in Mayfair and Belgravia and went out almost nightly to dinners, balls and soirées until the hours. Compare this with Bryan Johnson, the longevity guru who shuns anything that might dent his sleep score. We might call this “lazy” today, but Samuel is wiser than this: he points out that for those elites, personal and professional life were fused, and socializing was itself work.

Not everything about Victorian elites was good. There is virtue in working hard and our elites are probably much more apt at driving scientific advancements. That being said, there were distinct advantages to the Victorian way of being. What were these?

1. Victorian elite culture created a tight community at the top of a big society. The elite functioned like a village held together by sentiment and shared memory (and status competition). This helped them coordinate to work to the benefit of the country, which was also their own benefit.

2. The extended socialising and emphasis on creating a common culture created unity. Aristocrats and new money, Anglicans, Nonconformists, Jews and Catholics (except the Irish) were absorbed into one elite. Britain avoided the counter-elites and internal conflicts seen in the US South, Spain, France and Germany. To draw a parallel to today, where culture wars have deracinated our public spaces, elite non-uniformity can be very bad.

3. The Victorians paid people in prestige rather than money, and this strengthened state capacity. Local government, magistracies and Parliament were unpaid, and often costly, since MPs funded their own elections. Yet the most talented and wealthy competed for these roles, because their peers would esteem them for it. Modern states, by contrast, struggle to attract talent to poorly paid public posts. Without a common culture that confers prestige on public service, the talented drift to the private sector and state institutions decay, creating a negative feedback cycle.

4. Restraint in politics. Drawing on Bagehot, Samuel suggests that politicians sharing one social world may have been less inclined to destructive opposition, demagoguery or brinkmanship.

Read more about Victorian Elites and their habits in Wise Samuel's full piece!

The elites of Victorian Britain got up late, drank ceaselessly, worked short hours, partied through the night, and knew nothing about science, technology or engineering. And yet, by their own lights, they were hugely effective.

https://t.co/TvbuWtaPRJ

The Victorians are often held up as a model against the supposedly soft, feckless, humanities-educated elites of today. But I argue that the genius of their system may have been its drastic weighting towards soft skills, team-building and intra-elite networking:

- A Victorian’s gentleman’s office hours typically began about 11am and finished about 5pm, including a multi-course lunch with wine.

- Upper-class Victorians drank ceaselessly. Conduct guides recommended four or five glasses of wine at dinner *for married women*. Port was often served in pints.

- Party culture was intense and nocturnal. Balls started at about 10pm, peaked after 1am, and continued till dawn. During the social season, bankers, judges and politicians might go to several balls per week.

- Elite Victorians learnt almost no STEM at school or university. At least half of class time was given over to ancient languages, often as much as 80 percent. One leading educationalist remarked that it was not worth teaching science to gentlemen because it does not involve ‘continued reasoning’.

- Sports and character formation were valued far above transmitting facts. A top headmaster described his school’s priorities as ‘First – character, second – physique, third – intelligence, fourth – manners, fifth – information’.

This cannot have made elite Victorians more productive individually, but maybe the dense social and emotional network it created helped them to work as a sort of extended team. 

Perhaps we should think again about what makes groups of people effective.

Really important read. My own take:

I think that the question of consciousness and particularly the moral worth of consciousness doesn't really make sense outside of biological organisms evolved in the way we did. 

A simple way to visualise this: I think there could be surface level correlates of consciousness that nonetheless don't map to anything we would register as human experience. 

When a human says they're in pain we react to this because we assume all the associated states of this condition to be true. ln this case , the sensation of pain and the desire to avoid it, that is inherent to most biological organisms, since pain evolved specifically to teach us to avoid the thing causing pain. If an LLM says they're  in pain, we shouldn't assume the machinery that translates that into a sensation that is negative just exists. And I think we are prone to assuming that, because of a sort of cognitive illusion. The cognitive illusion arises because it simply doesn't happen in the natural world that things that speak and say they're in pain would not be humans. So our brains are very prone to assuming that the entire machinery is there. 

I cannot discount that a future version of LLMs might in some way have moral worth, but I think we should be very much aware of our cognitive biases and that animism is dangerous in and of itself. Dangerous to humans, that is. 

I think we should cross that bridge when (if) it arises.

Do you think the (new) building on the left should look more like the neighbouring one on the right?

I suspect most people do, but there's a widespread idea within historical preservation that any new/necessary additions to historic buildings/structures should be distinct and modern.

The idea dates back to the 60s where modernism was on the rise and was codified in something called 'The Venice Charter.'

"Article 9: New work should bear the mark of its own time. When restoration requires additional work, it should be distinguishable from the historic composition and carry a contemporary stamp.

This idea still influences planning today. Many people will assume that Brighton and Hove Council opted to go for the design on the left for reasons of cost/maintenance.

But, in fact, it was a deliberate decision.

Here's a quote from the planning officer: "A conscious effort had been made to make the design of the new lift different from the existing, allowing the older lift to retain prominence in the terrace."

What do you prefer?

China has become the most important manufacturing economy in the world because it is a continent-sized Silicon Valley.

https://t.co/QGdeeqmsEi

Every Chinese city govt acts as a VC firm trying to create clusters in its region, because it has both the means and incentive to do so.

Local govts generate their revenues, nearly all of which they keep, from selling leases on land and from stakes they have taken in local companies, which together allow them to capture economic spillovers.

Chinese officials have their entire careers graded and determined by how much growth they have been able to create in the areas they run. Career progression is determined according to a great tournament that pits official against official and gives promotions to whoever has grown their region the most. If they don’t reach a certain stage by a certain age they are blocked from promotion forever.

This is why so many economic clusters have centred on Chinese cities, for high- and low-tech products alike. Shaodong makes 70% of the entire world's cigarette lighters; Danyang makes half of the world's spectacle lenses; Zheng'an makes 1/7 of the world's guitars; Datang a third of its socks.

Whereas many of the West’s most important city governments capture only a small amount of the spillovers from successful clusters, and thus have very little reason to foster them, in China, they get a huge amount of the upside and can re-invest it in further growth. This also gives them a great incentive to solve problems for companies, like when Shanghai's govt got Tesla's factory there built even faster than Elon himself had expected (and twice as fast as his Fremont, CA factory).

But this is not some exotic 'oriental' innovation – this is how America used to do things when it grew fastest, in the 1950s, 1960s, and early 1970s. Catching up with China on advanced manufacturing does not require a wise and strategic approach, let alone authoritarianism or the end of democracy. It may just mean fixing city government. 

This is why I care so much about local  in Britain and America: if we give our own local governments the same incentives and means to grow, the crazily dysfunctional entities we have become used to may be transformed into corporation-like bodies that are ruthlessly focused on making their cities rich, safe and prosperous.

Read more in Works in Progress https://t.co/QGdeeqmsEi

Nearly everyone in the West focuses on China's Five Year Plans as the reasons for its manufacturing success, concluding that more central economic planning is needed. 

This is the exactly WRONG lesson. The country's success comes because its cities all compete with each other intensely, as something akin to vertically integrated corporations that are completely obsessed with local economic growth.

Its incredible manufacturing industry is based on local clusters that local govts nurture and invest in, and collect a lot of the returns from through property fees and taxes. These govts are *much* closer to local needs than Western local govts are, and can focus on speed of building and iteration above all, which are critical for manufacturing.

*This* is why local government matters in Britain and America, where it is almost completely broken and dysfunctional. Where local spillovers matter, as in manufacturing, you need some kind of entity that can internalise the positive externalities of economic activity. China is proof that with the right incentives and tax powers, local governments can become machines for economic growth, intervening and clearing the way for development.

What do a cutting-edge bone implant and Mrs Potts from Beauty and the Beast have in common? Both are made from porcelain, a material humans first made over 3,000 years ago and are still reinventing today.

https://t.co/gv0ZeRL8Pa

We focus on advances in computing, but the world around us has been transformed just as much by materials science. And within this already underrated field sits an even more underrated material. Plenty of people have heard of semiconductors, but almost no one thinks about porcelain. For @WorksInProgressMag, @CharlesCMann wrote about its remarkable journey:

- Porcelain is basically an ancient nanotechnology. 3000 years ago, Chinese potters found that firing a white clay called kaolin to around 1,200°C transformed it completely: its crystals get rebuilt, producing a material that is hard, dense, and sometimes translucent. Nobody knew why it worked at the time: they discovered it by trial and error.

- Europeans prized porcelain immensely – but had no clue had to make it. When porcelain arrived in Europe in the 12th century, it was so superior to European ceramics that aristocrats called it "white gold." But despite attempting to reverse-engineer it, Europeans failed to create porcelain for centuries.

- Fake it until you make porcelain. Böttger, an alchemist imprisoned in the early 1700s for falsely claiming to make gold, was set to work with a legitimate scientist on making porcelain. Remarkably, the scientist succeeded where others had failed for centuries, creating the first European porcelain cup. But he did not live to profit: ever the liar, Böttger claimed his discovery for himself.

- Less slippery when wet. Innovation in materials science picked up again in the 20th century and continues to this day, producing Porcelain 3.0. Today, porcelain can be found across a surprising number of household objects: from kitchen countertops to tiles that become less slippery when wet, which also makes them safer.

- The most futuristic use of all: researchers can now 3D-print porous porcelain scaffolds to repair damaged bone. The advantage is that blood vessels and bone cells grow into the scaffold’s tiny openings, while the scaffold slowly dissolves as new bone replaces it, allowing a bone-like natural structure to persist.

Porcelain has already gone from fragile imperial teacups to artificial joints and scaffolds that help bone regrow. But its 3000 year long story is far from over: expect this underrated material to play new roles in everything from medicine to architecture in the coming decades!

I think Andy Burnham should champion the idea of 'municipal socialism': having utilities owned by local governments, primarily combined authorities, rather than the national monopoly that nationalisation usually entails. This may already be what he is planning, but he hasn't really said so yet. 

Nationalised monopoly fails for many reasons:

- It creates entities that are too big to fail, so they can waste large amounts of money while being subsidised from public funds.

- It gives people no comparison point to see if a certain industry is being well-run, so bad outcomes end up being treated like bad weather.

- It prevents the public companies themselves from learning from other companies, because they only have other countries to learn from where circumstances might be very different.

- It creates very weak political feedback mechanisms, because your vote on whether the trains are being run well is bundled with your vote on, eg, tax policy and foreign policy.

- It engenders short-termism, because voters are less forward looking than private investors, so there is more scope to take long-term degradation of service for short-term benefits. (This is happening with TfL's fare freeze right now.)

Municipal ownership does not solve all these problems, but it can maintain more accountability and some of the elements of competition that national monopoly does not have.

There is more room for experimentation and learning because different municipalities try different policies, and can copy the successes from each other. The Oyster Card and contactless card payments were a good example of this by TfL. Manchester's bus privatisation scheme was scrapped in part by looking at the success of London's approach to buses, where delivery is outsourced to multiple private companies but services are designed by a single authority and provided under one brand.

The 'too big to fail' problem is smaller, because municipal governments can face a harder budget constraint than national government, though bailouts undermine this. Those that want to subsidise services have to draw on a narrower tax base. In fact, well-run services can raise revenues for local governments, as many locally-owned tramways did in the 19th and early 20th Centuries. Local authorities are more accountable for failures and get more credit for successes than national governments would be.

Internationally, successful examples of public ownership of utilities are often owned by municipalities. This is true in much of the United States, where water is mostly municipally owned rather than private, and in France, where most public services are owned by local governments, who then offer contracts to companies to handle the actual delivery. The Bee network and London buses operate on the same basis.

Historically in Britain, trams, electricity and gas were all mostly run by small local companies and local governments before the 1940s–70s. Municipally-owned gas networks were highly profitable for Birmingham under Joseph Chamberlain. There were still nearly 200 different water boards across England by 1970!

We use 'nationalisation' as a byword for 'public ownership', but there is little reason for most of these things to be nationalised monopolies. Much of the drive towards nationalised monopoly in the 20th Century was inspired by a mistaken belief that economies of scale would drive the biggest improvements in productivity, inspired by the apparent success of the USSR and large conglomerates in Germany and the USA. It is clear today that experimentation via trial and error is extremely valuable, and losing it is one of the big costs of monopoly.

'Municipalisation' would, for example, mean overhauling the Great British Railways policy which by default puts commuter lines in Surrey into the same administration that runs the West Midlands Cross-City Line, the East Coast Main Line, and commuter networks in Manchester, Leeds and Liverpool. There are some provisions for lines going into municipal control, but the default is to stop the next Mayor of Greater Manchester from running the region's commuter trains and London from absorbing more lines into the Overground.

Public ownership has many flaws, but some of them are avoidable by looking beyond the 1940s and 1970s for how to do it. 'Municipal socialism' allows for much greater learning and feedback loops, and would hugely strengthen devolution by making local government responsible for things that directly matter to their electorates rather than having them run by a single inert national monopoly.

Nearly everyone in the West focuses on China's Five Year Plans as the reasons for its manufacturing success, concluding that more central economic planning is needed. 

This is the exactly WRONG lesson. The country's success comes because its cities all compete with each other intensely, as something akin to vertically integrated corporations that are completely obsessed with local economic growth.

Its incredible manufacturing industry is based on local clusters that local govts nurture and invest in, and collect a lot of the returns from through property fees and taxes. These govts are *much* closer to local needs than Western local govts are, and can focus on speed of building and iteration above all, which are critical for manufacturing.

*This* is why local government matters in Britain and America, where it is almost completely broken and dysfunctional. Where local spillovers matter, as in manufacturing, you need some kind of entity that can internalise the positive externalities of economic activity. China is proof that with the right incentives and tax powers, local governments can become machines for economic growth, intervening and clearing the way for development.

There is no good reason for mosquitoes to exist in wealthy countries today.

New technologies can get rid of the mosquito species that cause diseases like dengue, yellow fever, and malaria; and others can prevent them from carrying those diseases.
https://t.co/CddUFByGZA

So why do mosquitoes still exist? 

In a new article for Works in Progress, Maya Rosen explains how state incapacity and risk aversion led to over a decade of delays and billions of unnecessary bites in the United States.

Oxitec, for example, engineered an Aedes aegypti mosquito in such a way that its female offspring would die before adulthood. Through sustained releases, they showed they could reduce local mosquito populations by 80% or more, in field trials.

They sought approval from the USDA in 2010, which then passed it to the FDA, which passed it to the EPA. In 2020, the EPA allowed them to conduct limited field trials in the Florida Keys. Two years ago, their experimental permit expired, and they still need another review before it can be used routinely. Their proposed field trial in California was withdrawn after public opposition.

Another company, MosquitoMate, developed a technique involving Wolbachia, which also suppresses local mosquitoes. They then spent over fifteen years working through the system before finally receiving commercial registration nationwide in 2024.

It seems that, sometimes, the barrier to getting rid of diseases isn’t technology at all. It’s policy and political will.

New products shouldn’t get stuck in regulatory review for so long, especially if the delays are about basic questions like which agency has oversight over the product, rather than testing for safety.

Though some of those uncertainties were being addressed, the broader changes haven’t materialized. After Biden’s 2022 executive order, the agencies planned to update how their coordinated framework was implemented. But Trump rescinded the order last year.

Meanwhile, the EPA unit that reviews new mosquito control products is still a small office backlogged in reviewing a wide range of products.

Mosquitoes are a policy choice. We can get rid of them. Will we choose to?

In a blast from the past, Britain’s competition regulator has proposed designating Microsoft’s business software, including Windows, Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams, as having “strategic market status.”

It's like 1998 all over again, except this time the CMA is proposing to regulate a single company precisely in the part of the economy where competition has never been stronger: AI. These kinds of fiddly regulatory interventions are bound to scare away investment and turn the entire scheme into a laughing stock.

SMS status lets the CMA impose bespoke conduct requirements on how Microsoft designs, bundles and sells its products. This gives the regulator broad discretion to direct how software used by more than a million UK organisations is allowed to operate.

The CMA's complaint is that the products are integrated, something CMA-commissioned research found businesses see as a “key benefit” and “relatively good value for money” and “more cost-effective than buying and managing separate licences.” Put plainly, people keep using Microsoft because the products work well together and they’re good value. This is very far from a market failure that requires intervention. It’s also a sector facing immense disruption in the era of AI-led software development.

What's particularly mad is that Copilot is in scope too, even though ChatGPT has more than 1 billion weekly users, Gemini has more than 1 billion monthly users, and in UK workplaces, only about one in ten Microsoft Office users use Copilot. Gemini, Claude and ChatGPT together already have roughly as many workplace users as Copilot, after just two or three years. Just a year ago, the CMA kept Gemini out of Google’s designation because AI was moving too fast to call.

The CMA’s legal test is meant to ask whether Microsoft’s position will be entrenched over the next five years. Five years ago, ChatGPT didn’t exist. Anyone confident about who will lead workplace AI in 2031 should be running a hedge fund, not a regulator.

What's also interesting is that, despite the promises made when this regime was created, this regulation isn’t even well-targeted. The CMA’s real concern, from its cloud market investigation, was meant to be Microsoft’s cloud software licensing. Instead of targeting this issue directly, the CMA has opted for the widest possible net: five separate markets bundled into one ecosystem. The result is that nothing will be done till at least February 2027, and even then, conduct requirements aren't yet specified, which will require further consultations, delaying action well into 2027.

Britain wants to be the best place in the world to build and adopt AI. Preemptively regulating the AI tools businesses are only just starting to use is a strange way to get there.

We’re delighted to announce that the one and only @tylercowen, our internet writing sensei, is joining Works in Progress as a regular contributor. 

https://t.co/NuvOFqfPin

His first column is about Brazilian food, and like everything Tyler writes, it’s packed with hidden gems that make it much more than a food story.

Some of the nicest tidbits: on her first trip to Brazil, his daughter declared she had “never had a banana before” –  this is how good Brazilian bananas are, apparently. 
And Tyler and a well-traveled friend from Modena (of all places) agreed that Brazil is the third-best country in the world for Italian food, behind only Italy and Japan. If an Italian says that, we’d better trust him!

But as always with Tyler, he manages to draw larger lessons from apparently mundane and object-level stories. So, in a short read, we learn much more than just the fact that Brazilian food is really good.

First, food can be seen as a progress story. Brazil’s agricultural yields rival, and sometimes beat, those of the US, even though Brazil is a much poorer country. Abundant fertile land, high productivity, and short supply chains make ingredients plentiful and fresh. Tyler’s regret is that the rest of Brazil’s economy hasn’t embraced technology the way its food sector has.

We also learn how immigration shapes Brazilian cuisine. Brazil has roughly 2 million citizens of Japanese descent, which makes it arguably the best place outside Japan for Japanese food. Tyler had a 15-course omakase at a Michelin-starred São Paulo restaurant for $110, booked just half an hour ahead. Brazil is also home to about 30 million people of Italian descent, the largest Italian diaspora in the world, which goes a long way to explain why his Italian friend was so satisfied with the food.

The whole column is a delight, so do read it in full!

The government's Renters' Rights Bill looks like it will be a catastrophe, inadvertently introducing rent controls and reducing the supply of housing even more. It is the clearest evidence that the whole British state that has brought it about is completely broken: 

• Written by the civil service
• Introduced by the Tories
• Passed by Labour and the Lib Dems
• Cheered on by the mainstream media

The bill's core provision is to eliminate "no-fault evictions". Many understand this to mean evictions during a rental lease. In fact, this is already impossible. What the new bill does is to stop landlords from being able to regain their property after a lease has expired. 

This means that renting a property to someone now means that they get to live in that property indefinitely. A landlord can only evict them if they are selling the property, or plan to move into it themselves, or if a tribunal gives them permission after ruling against the tenant for bad behaviour.

Within these indefinite contracts, rent increases will be capped at whatever the 'market rate' is determined to be by a tribunal. Tribunals will not be able to *raise* rents, as they currently can and often do – only lower them or keep them where they are. The only risk to a tenant is that their challenge is deemed "vexatious".

Not only will rent increases *within* contracts be controlled by courts, rents for *new* contracts will also be controlled by them. Tenants will be entitled to agree a rent, move in, and then immediately take their landlord to a rent tribunal on the grounds that the rent they have just agreed to is "too high".

Rent tribunals will thus have the power to control all rents. All rents will be set under the threat of a tribunal intervening. There will be no "market rate", so the tribunal will have no independent "market rate" to refer to.

A tenant who challenges a rent increase will have their rent frozen at the old, lower rate while their challenge is ongoing (which could take over a year). Like the Building Safety Regulator right now, tribunals are likely to be extremely backlogged, creating huge delays where tenants do not have to pay their new higher rents, if they ever do. Tenants will have huge incentives to challenge nearly all rent increases. 

We have already seen how bad courts are at ruling on prices, eg in cases where Next's shop workers have been given the same pay as factory floor workers, and in Birmingham where the council was forced to pay £760m to care workers and teaching assistants because a court decided that these roles were equivalent to jobs like rubbish collectors.

All this amounts to rent controls. These are terrible for many reasons.

1. They will cause landlords to sell up and leave the market. This is both to avoid the risk of being stuck with a bad tenant, and because once the rent has been kept artificially low by a rent tribunal, landlords will be losing money compared to just selling into private owner-occupation.

Rental properties allow for easy doubling up (housesharing) which is much messier under owner-occupation. The effective supply of housing is about to drop. In Ireland, postwar rent controls shrunk the rental market from 26% to 8% of the total housing stock in 40 years. In Britain, 1916–88, the share of properties available for rent went from 75% of the market to 10%.

2. They cause landlords to neglect their properties. Landlords receiving artificially-depressed rents for their properties have no incentive to maintain them. Rent controlled properties, famously, become neglected and fall into decay, as leaks, cracked plaster and broken windows are left unaddressed. The country's housing stock that remains in renting will decay. Our cities will become more decrepit.

3. They stop people from moving around for better jobs. We already have this effect with social housing, where huge amounts of inner London housing (30–40%!) are held by tenants in low wage jobs, or who have no job at all, instead of by people who could move to London to earn and produce more. This will happen to large swathes of the rental market too, stopping people from moving into prosperous cities where they could get better jobs.

4. They stop the supply of new homes for rent. Under rent controls, there is no incentive to build new homes for renting. Britain built essentially no private flats for rent between 1945 and the end of rent controls in 1988. The same was true in France between WWI when it introduced rent controls and the slow end of rent controls in the postwar era.

5. They push renters into the black market. To actually get a place to live, a lot of people will sidestep these new rules and rent informally, with none of the protections we currently have for renters like the deposit protection scheme. This is the sort of scenario that allows landlords to *really* exploit and steal from their tenants.

–

Do not assume that anyone involved with this knows what they're doing. We have already seen, in the case of the Building Safety Regulator and the second staircase regulations (brought in by the same Housing Secretary who designed this bill), how disastrous the consequences of well-intended but misconceived interventions in the housing market can be.

I always thought that the ancient Romans were tolerant about sexuality, until the rise of puritanical Christianity. Reading Kyle Harper, I learnt that this picture is not exactly false, but it is extraordinarily misleading:

https://t.co/PJO8UTGgiK

- Sexual penetration of a free Roman man was severely punished, possibly by death. Consenting to penetration was also seriously punished. Lesbianism was not criminalised, but was regarded with contempt.

- The one great subject of permissiveness was the penetration of enslaved people. Although relatively few people owned slaves, many prostitutes were enslaved and prostitution was ubiquitous, so coerced sex was widespread.

- In some parts of the empire, many married women probably seem to have worn face veils in public.

- There was not even theoretically a norm of male fidelity: although wives were required to be faithful to their husbands, the inverse was not even aspirationally true. 

- Early Christianity wrought a kind of revolution on ancient morality. All forms of sexuality apart from procreative sex within monogamous marriage were relentlessly and violently condemned, and even marital sex was allowed only rather grudgingly. In effect, the Christians extended to men the restrictions that had previously applied only to women.

- To a limited extent, they also extended the protections previously enjoyed by free men to other groups of people. Although the early Christian record on slavery is mostly very poor, they did introduce the first laws against the forcible prostitution of slaves. Transgressors were to be arrested and sent to the public mines, ‘which is’, the law ran, ‘less of a punishment than that of a woman who is seized by a pimp and compelled to endure the filth of an intercourse that she did not will’.

It is not clear how much behaviour actually changed in practice – the Christians were never able to get people to behave exactly as they wanted. But the change in official norms was revolutionary, and not quite the revolution I expected.

I'm grateful to Jonathan for writing this and very pleased to publish it in Works in Progress – he does great work, and I like him and respect his views immensely. I have two thoughts in response.

One is that I am not hugely compelled by people telling others what they should focus on. As long as you're not doing active harm to the world, it's fine to work on a less high-priority area than you could. Comparative advantage is not always easy to judge from outside and part of living a satisfying life is doing what you find most intrinsically interesting and rewarding. 

And entrepreneurship is *inherently* about working on things that other people underrate! There wouldn't be any opportunities for discovery if it was clear exactly what everyone should focus their time on.

(I don't have much time for people who complain that a handful of EAs are worried about shrimp welfare either, unless they are actually hurting the shrimp.)

Two: even if you concede Jonathan's argument that encouraging nice buildings and places does not instrumentally advance the cause of YIMBYism – we can agree to disagree – I think that it is a mistake to dismiss aesthetics as being trivial.

People want beauty and pleasure in their lives, not just boxes to sleep and work in. Cities should be amazing places to be, and the way they look and feel is a big part of that. The greatest cities I have been to are Paris, London, Tokyo, and New York, all of which are breathtakingly beautiful cities in their own way, even though some of them create that beautiful whole from various ugly parts arranged well. I think this is often true of parts of London, where individually ugly buildings nonetheless combine to make a beautiful skyline or street. The best places, like inner Paris and lower Manhattan, combine beautiful streetscapes with individually-beautiful buildings.

If you think too much about "units of housing" and not enough about which places people most want to live in and visit, you will miss a lot of what actually matters to people about the places they live and visit. It is a constant error to think that the "function" of buildings and cities does not include "being pleasant and looking nice".

This is all obviously subjective, but so are lots of other important things that still benefit from some form of collective decision making – pollution, noise, public order, the provision of public goods. The interesting meta-question to me is what institutions allow for the best ways to make these decisions and resolve conflicts between people.

“The Simpsons” was a beloved animated sitcom that ran for ten legendary seasons and concluded in 1999. The show was celebrated for what was widely perceived as a near perfect run that wrapped before it wore out its concept and overstayed its welcome.

Creator Matt Groening and showrunner James L. Brooks famously decided to bring the show to a conclusion after experiencing the negative audience reaction to the season 9 episode “The Principal and the Pauper,” in which it was revealed that the school’s principal was actually an impostor who had stolen the real Seymour Skinner’s identity.  Brooks did not want to sully the show’s legacy by doing a bunch of weird episodes as the franchise slid into mediocrity and cultural irrelevance, so the writers and cast decided instead to go out on top and end things on a high note.

However, because of its centrality in 90s pop culture, a long-running Internet joke is to pretend “The Simpsons” is still on the air, a premise that gets more absurd and deranged with each passing year. If this show were still producing new episodes, it would be in its 38th season now, and most of the voice cast would be in their 80s.

The joke is to imagine how distorted this charming show would have become if it had been stretched out to more than 800 episodes. Comedy posters on “weird Twitter” used to try to top each other by making up terrible ideas for what modern episodes of the show might be like.

For example, a viral 2012 tweet imagined an episode where Lady Gaga helps Lisa Simpson with her self esteem. In 2019, popular shitposter Megan Amram originated the premise of Bart Simpson becoming a men’s rights activist to protest a gender-swapped reboot of “Itchy and Scratchy.”

But perhaps the most elaborate Internet “Simpsons” joke was a 2017 YouTube mockumentary “The Problem With Apu,” in which the comedian Hari Kondabolu ironically pretended to be offended by the charming and innocuous convenience store owner character Apu. 

Everyone thought this was hilarious, especially since the show had been off the air for nearly two decades when the mockumentary was released. So, Twitter ran with the joke by pretending to “cancel” Apu, and the viral gag memorably resulted in the character’s voice actor, Hank Azaria, recognizing the meme by promising never to perform the character again, which everybody thought was really funny since Azaria had been retired for years.

Now, nearly a decade later, fans are pretending that the show — which has now been off the air longer than most people tweeting about it have been alive— has brought back the “cancelled” character with a new racially-appropriate voice actor. 

I actually don’t think this is that funny, and I kind of think the gag of pretending “The Simpsons” is still airing new episodes has overstayed its welcome, a mistake the actual show “The Simpsons” would never have made.

If you haven’t seen this 1990s classic, which — and I cannot emphasize this enough — ended after 10 seasons in 1999, you can watch all the episodes on Disney+ (except the one with Michael Jackson that got pulled from streaming).

CONFIRMED. Gas Standing Charges to be scrapped. I've just come out of a meeting with the Chancellor. The gas standing charge will be scrapped in 2027 (my guess, either for 1 Oct price cap or the 1 Jan 28 price cap). Having campaigned against the moral hazard of standing charges for years, I'm pleased.

It's currently £108 a year. That cost will be shifted onto unit rates. We don't know how much yet, but I suspect just under 1p per kwH.

The Chancellor also said he will be talking to Ofgem about how they get rid of the charge on electricity as well, but that is 'trickier' apparently and will take longer.

This is primarily about the price cap standing charges. There will still be an open market, so other firms can offer other forms of prices with or without the standing charge. My suspicion is that once it goes on the price cap, it will tend to be reduced on other tariffs as well.

As for those on fixes: if you get a fix now, the rate of your fix is fixed, so this should not affect it. You will pay what you pay and if it has standing charges they will continue (some asking if they should delay fixing because of this, no if a fix is right for you and will save you money, don't let this change that - this is about the structure of bills, as opposed to the actual costs on bills).

About 60% of people will pay less due to this, 40% more. My guesstimate is the dividing line will be somewhere around 12,500 kilowatt hours of gas (can't know until there is actual pricing). According to a study by Nesta, this switch would leave the majority of people in all income groups under £100,000 better off.

Of course, when this does come in, if we're still in the nightmare that we are right now, there will need to be support put in for vulnerable higher users, who will have to pay more. Though hopefully by then the mid-east will have calmed and energy prices lower. 
---------------

That's all long term. The biggest issue in energy right now is that we're expecting a 27% rise in the price cap in January. I asked the Chancellor whether he will be intervening on that. He told me I'd have to wait for the budget, but reading between the lines, yes, there will be an announcement today. 

Whether it's an increase in the Warm Home Discount, or whether it's council tax banned, or whether it's done via a payout for people in say council tax bands A-D as a proxy for household income as Rishi Sunak did who knows.
